Formulation:
- Concise formulation: Young adult with known atopic background (asthma, hay fever; possible eczema) presenting with acute exertional-onset shortness of breath, wheeze and cough over 2–3 days. Predisposing factors: pre-existing asthma and atopy. Precipitating factors: exercise (symptoms began while running), possible viral or allergen trigger. Perpetuating factors: increased reliance on short-acting beta-agonist with reported reduced effect and an interval since formal asthma review (~2 years). Protective factors: patient engaged with clinician and arranged further GP review. Current presentation most consistent with an acute asthma exacerbation; alternative/associated contributors include viral bronchitis and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction per DDx.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Acute asthma exacerbation
- Patient Goal(s): Not recorded
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Relieve acute bronchospasm and wheeze
  - Prevent deterioration and avoid need for emergency care
  - Reassess asthma control and optimize preventer therapy
- Actions (Patient):
  - Use blue (salbutamol) inhaler as needed; interim guidance given to use up to every 2–4 hours if symptomatic (per clinician instructions).
  - Increase brown preventer (Clenil/beclometasone) to 4 puffs twice daily while awaiting GP review (as advised).
  - Monitor symptoms; seek immediate emergency care (A&E) if breathing worsens despite interim measures.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Arrange face-to-face GP review within next few days for chest examination and current peak flow measurement.
  - At review, perform chest auscultation and objective peak flow; consider oral corticosteroid course and/or antibiotics depending on clinical findings.
  - Provide formal asthma review, consider adjustment of baseline preventer regimen and provide inhaler technique review.

Secondary Problem: Viral respiratory infection / bronchitis (triggering asthma symptoms)
- Patient Goal(s): Not recorded
- Clinical Goal(s:
  - Identify and treat any infective trigger if present
  - Minimize impact on asthma control)
- Actions (Patient):
  - Symptomatic care (fluids, rest) — general advice inferred from usual care but not explicitly detailed; follow clinician instructions at GP review.
  - Report any new systemic features (fever, worsening cough, purulent sputum).
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Assess for infective features at face-to-face review; prescribe antibiotics only if clinically indicated.
  - Consider short course oral corticosteroids if asthma exacerbation judged moderate–severe.

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Inhaler use and interim dosing changes (increase Clenil to 4 puffs twice daily; salbutamol up to every 2–4 hours if required).
  - Need for timely GP face-to-face review and chest examination/peak flow.
  - Clear instruction to attend A&E if breathing deteriorates before review.
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - Increasing breathlessness or wheeze
  - Need to use salbutamol frequently (every 2–4 hours or more)
  - Progressive limitation on walking/exertion or inability to speak in full sentences (not specifically stated but implied by clinician instruction to seek A&E if breathing worsens)
- Coping Strategies: Not recorded
